title: Concentration–time graphs, half-life and clock reactions; Rate-determining step and mechanisms
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: KN05#t1 term and clue written for the game; KN06#t4 term and clue written for the game; KN06#t2 term and clue written for the game; KN06#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: KN05#N.8b, KN06#N.3b, KN05#N.12a, KN06#N.5, KN06#N.8, KN06#N.9, KN06#N.13.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Half-life
items.clue: The time taken to lose 50% of what is left of a reactant.

items.label: Molecularity
items.clue: The number of particles that collide, or break up, in one elementary stage.

items.label: Intermediate
items.clue: Forms in one stage and is used up in a later one; it sits at an energy minimum.

items.label: Rate-determining step
items.clue: The slowest stage of a mechanism, which limits how fast the whole reaction goes.

questions.stem: A hypothetical compound, A, decomposes in a reaction that is first order with respect to A. At a certain temperature the rate constant is k = 0.020 s⁻¹. In one trial at this temperature the initial concentration of A is 0.80 M. What is [A] after 25 s?

The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in the presence of iodide ions is proposed to occur by the following mechanism. Step 1: H₂O₂(aq) + I⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) + IO⁻(aq). Step 2: H₂O₂(aq) + IO⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) + O₂(g) + I⁻(aq). Which statement correctly identifies the roles of I⁻ and IO⁻ in this mechanism?

options.text: I⁻ acts as a catalyst, and IO⁻ is an intermediate.
IO⁻ is a catalyst, and I⁻ is an intermediate.
I⁻ and IO⁻ are both intermediates in the steps.
I⁻ and IO⁻ both act as catalysts in the steps.

questions.explanation: I⁻ is used in step 1 and re-formed in step 2: catalyst. IO⁻ is formed in step 1 and used in step 2: intermediate.

questions.stem: A hypothetical compound X decomposes at constant temperature. Results: t = 0, 200, 400, 600 s; [X] = 0.640, 0.320, 0.160, 0.080 M. A new trial at the same temperature starts at [X] = 0.320 M. How long does [X] take to fall to 0.080 M?
questions.explanation: [X] halves every 200 s, whatever the start: first order. 0.320 → 0.160 → 0.080 is two halvings: 400 s.

questions.stem: The reaction 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g) has the experimentally determined rate law rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. A student claims that this rate law shows that the reaction occurs in a single elementary step. Which evaluation of the claim is best?

options.text: Doubtful: a single step would need a rare collision of three particles at once.
Justified: orders equal to the coefficients show that a reaction is a single step.
Justified: a balanced equation shows the particles that collide in the reaction.
Doubtful: two molecules of one substance, NO, do not react in the same step.

questions.explanation: One step would fit the rate law, but it does not prove it. It would need three particles to collide at once, which is rare.

questions.stem: The overall equation for a reaction is 2X + Y → X₂Y. The experimental rate equation is rate = k[X][Y]. Which mechanism is consistent with both?

options.text: Step 1: X + Y → XY (slow). Step 2: XY + X → X₂Y (fast).
Step 1: X + X → X₂ (slow). Step 2: X₂ + Y → X₂Y (fast).
Step 1: X + Y ⇌ XY (fast). Step 2: XY + X → X₂Y (slow).
Step 1: X + Y → XY (slow). Step 2: XY + Y → XY₂ (fast).

questions.explanation: The steps add to 2X + Y → X₂Y, and the slow first step has one X and one Y: rate = k[X][Y].

questions.stem: A proposed mechanism for the hypothetical reaction 2 A(g) + B(g) → C(g) has two steps. Step 1: A + A ⇌ A₂ (fast, reversible). Step 2: A₂ + B → C (slow). The rate law predicted by the mechanism is rate = k[A]²[B]. Which statement explains why [A] appears in this rate law although A is not a reactant in the slow step?

options.text: Step 1 comes before step 2, and the first step of a mechanism sets the rate law.
A is a reactant in the overall equation, and overall reactants appear in the rate law.
Step 1 ties the amount of A₂ to the amount of A, and A₂ is a reactant in the slow step.
Step 1 and step 2 both count, and the rate law combines the reactants of both steps.

questions.stem: A hypothetical reaction occurs by a three-step mechanism. Relative to the reactants, the energies of the species along the reaction coordinate are: first transition state, +30 kJ/mol; first intermediate, +20 kJ/mol; second transition state, +105 kJ/mol; second intermediate, −10 kJ/mol; third transition state, +40 kJ/mol; products, −70 kJ/mol. Which step is the rate-determining step, and why?

options.text: Step 1, because the first step of a mechanism sets the rate of the reaction
Step 2, because its activation energy is the largest of the three steps
Step 1, because its products are higher in energy than its reactants
Step 3, because it has the largest energy change of the three steps
